newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Oil-rich C. Asia's trade hurt by Afghan turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Oil-rich C. Asia's trade hurt by Afghan turmoil.

text.p: Renewed turmoil in Afghanistan appears to have dashed the long-standing hopes of its neighbours in the former Soviet Union to link their Central Asian countries firmly to southern Asian markets.

Investors initially hoped the radical Islamic Taleban militia's seizure of the Afghan capital Kabul last month could presage a strong government which could open up bandit-infested roads between central Asia and ports on the Arabian Sea.
But with Afghan fighters again at each others' throats, prospects of a healthy flow of oil and goods between Central Asia and Western markets through Afghanistan have dimmed.
Pakistan, hurting at Iran and Turkey's headstart into Central Asia's potentially oil-rich markets, would have had the most to gain from a stable Afghanistan.
"Instability in Afghanistan denies us our shortest approach to Central Asia," said a Pakistani diplomat based in the Kazakh capital Almaty.
To avoid Afghanistan's troubled highways, Pakistan's goods have to follow follow torturous mountain roads through Kashgar in China and over the Tien Shan mountains into Kyrgyzstan

Fighting between the Taleban and ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood currently blocks the Salang highway northwest of Kabul, the only proper road linking it to Central Asia via Afghanistan.

Turkmenistan, the United States and Pakistan, keen to break Russia's virtual monopoly on trade and energy exports from Central Asia, want to build oil and gas pipelines from Turkmenistan to Pakistan through Afghanistan.
The United States imposes trade sanctions on Tehran, which it accuses of sponsoring terrorism, and Afghanistan looked to be a way of sidestepping Iran.

America's Unocal Corp and Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil Co aim to raise over $4 billion to build the Turkmen-Pakistani pipelines, which would be able to pump a million barrels a day of Central Asian crude out to the Arabian Sea.

"The initial reaction was that a Taleban victory would make things easier (for the pipeline), that there would be less people to negotiate with," said a Western diplomat based in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat.

But most of the region's oil frontiersmen say Afghanistan is still too risky. "Most people think it's a long shot, a 'pipe dream' if you like," said an oil executive based in Kazakhstan. "Most expect more violence, more civil war."
A majority in the oil business still see Iran as the shortest, safest export route for Central Asian states across one of the world's trickiest geopolitical faultlines.

The only pipeline actually being built in the region will carry gas from Turkmenistan to northern Iran. Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov has called the pipeline a first link to markets in Turkey and Europe.
The Afghan route is not helped by Central Asian leaders' own deep distrust of the Taleban's radical brand of Islam, which they fear could spark unrest inside their own fragile republics.
Meanwhile, the Taleban's reverses suit Russia, Central Asia's old colonial overlord, which is determined to keep a tight grip on the taps to Central Asian oil.
